First 3-axis molecular fabric weaves itself

ScienceNow! short on a peer-reviewed Nature Version of Record.

Title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
Authors: Mengbin Wang, Shuai Fang, Xuedong Xiao, Zhewen Guo, Tianyu Shan, Han Han, Chun Tang, Ding Xiao, Guangguo Wang, Zhongwen Liu, Bohan Zhao, Shang Li, Ming Liu, Yan-Fang Wang, Jinbo Li, Ming Li, Liya Chen, Zhenglin Du, Chong Yao, Yizhao Du, Jiyong Liu, J. Fraser Stoddart, Jonathan L. Sessler, Guangfeng Li, Feihe Huang (25 authors)
Journal: Nature (published online 2026-11-04; Article Published 04 November 2026)
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8

Until now, molecular weaving mostly used straight strands and two-axis patterns — like ordinary cloth at the molecular scale. Making a true three-axis weave from nonlinear building blocks has been rare and hard to study in detail.

Wang, Fang, Xiao, Guo, Shan, and colleagues report a two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven polymer network — a fabric-like polymer sheet woven along three axes. They build it by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into the woven structure through dative boron–nitrogen polymerization.

The material shows topological chirality and robust mechanical properties. As a porous solid, it can also separate representative aromatic compounds from aliphatic ones.

That shows how higher-order triaxial woven topologies can tune material behavior and adds another topological design route for functional materials. Limitation: this is still an early-stage materials demonstration; separations were shown for representative mixtures, not proven at industrial scale.

Nature, 2026.

AI hunch, not proven: If triaxial molecular weaves can be tuned for selective pores, they might someday help chemical separations — but this paper did not test industrial processes. What do you think?
